title: Helm, Kustomize & Package Management
summary: Managing Kubernetes manifests at scale, across environments, without hand-editing a growing pile of near-duplicate YAML.

slides.markdown:
One app might need a Deployment, a Service, a ConfigMap, an Ingress, and an HPA — and you need that whole set three times over, for dev, staging, and prod, with just a handful of values actually different each time. Hand-copying YAML per environment means every shared fix has to be repeated N times, and drift creeps in silently.

Helm and Kustomize both solve this, from opposite directions: Helm **templates** the differences out; Kustomize **patches** a shared base to produce them.

slides.subTitle: Charts, values, releases
slides.markdown:
A Helm **chart** is a package of templated YAML plus a `values.yaml` defining defaults. Installing a chart with a specific set of values produces a **release** — a named, versioned, tracked instance of that chart in a cluster (`helm install payments-prod ./chart -f prod-values.yaml`).

Helm keeps release history, so `helm rollback payments-prod 3` reverts the *entire set* of rendered manifests to an earlier release revision in one command — not just one resource.

slides.subTitle: The templating engine
slides.markdown:
Templates use Go templating with values substituted in at render time:

```yaml
# templates/deployment.yaml
spec:
  replicas: {{ .Values.replicaCount }}
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
        - image: "{{ .Values.image.repo }}:{{ .Values.image.tag }}"
```

`helm template ./chart -f prod-values.yaml` renders the final YAML without installing anything — the right way to inspect exactly what a given values file produces before it ever touches a cluster.

slides.subTitle: Overlay-based customization
slides.markdown:
Kustomize starts from a plain `base/` directory of ordinary, valid YAML — no template syntax, no `{{ }}` — and layers **overlays** (`overlays/prod/`) that patch specific fields: bump replica count, change an image tag, add a label. `kubectl apply -k overlays/prod` applies the base plus that overlay's patches.

Because the base is real YAML, `kubectl apply -f base/` works standalone too — there's no templating engine to have installed, which is why Kustomize ships built into `kubectl` itself.

Templating vs patching is the real dividing line.

| | Helm | Kustomize |
|---|---|---|
| Approach | Templating (`{{ }}` placeholders) | Patching (overlay a plain YAML base) |
| Packaging | Versioned charts, shareable via repos | No package format — just directories |
| Best fit | Distributing a reusable app (e.g. installing Prometheus) | Customizing YAML you own, per environment |
| Built into kubectl | No, separate CLI | Yes (`kubectl apply -k`) |

Many teams use both: Helm to install third-party charts, Kustomize to patch their own app's manifests per environment.

A **chart repository** is an HTTP-served index of packaged charts (`.tgz` files) plus an `index.yaml` of versions — Artifact Hub aggregates public ones. `helm install repo/chart --version x.y.z` pulls a specific version. Chart **semantic versioning** matters: a chart's version bumps independently of the app's image tag, since templates or defaults can change without the app changing.

Pinning a chart version in CI is the same discipline as pinning any dependency — an unpinned `helm upgrade` can silently pull in unreviewed template changes.

slides.subTitle: One chart, three environments
slides.markdown:
One chart, three thin values files:

```yaml
# values-dev.yaml
replicaCount: 1
resources: { requests: { cpu: "100m" } }

# values-prod.yaml
replicaCount: 5
resources: { requests: { cpu: "500m" } }
autoscaling: { enabled: true, maxReplicas: 20 }
```

`helm upgrade --install app ./chart -f values-prod.yaml` deploys prod's shape from the exact same templates dev uses — the *only* thing that differs between environments lives in these small values files, not in duplicated manifests.

slides.subTitle: A release drifting from what's applied
slides.markdown:
**The wrong belief:** "if Helm says the release succeeded, the cluster matches the chart."

**Why it breaks:** a manual `kubectl edit`/`patch` against a Helm-managed resource changes the live object but not Helm's recorded release manifest. State now disagrees, and the *next* `helm upgrade` can silently revert that manual change.

**The correct model:** treat Helm-managed resources as only editable through Helm; if a manual patch is unavoidable, reconcile it back into the chart's values afterward.

slides.subTitle: Why a failed upgrade can leave a release stuck
slides.markdown:
Helm **hooks** (`pre-install`, `pre-upgrade`, `post-upgrade`) run extra Jobs around a release — a schema migration before the new Pods start, a smoke test after. If a `pre-upgrade` hook Job fails, Helm marks the release `failed` and stops before touching the Deployment at all, which is exactly the point: don't roll new code out against a database migration that didn't finish.

A release stuck `pending-upgrade` after a crashed `helm` client (not a hook failure, just a dropped connection) is a different problem — Helm's own lock wasn't released. `helm rollback` won't budge it; the fix is `helm rollback --force` or, in older Helm versions, manually patching the release Secret's status before retrying.
